result.summary: Cadmus is told by Delphi to follow a cow, founds Thebes, kills Ares' dragon and sows its teeth, then marries Harmonia. The section then follows his children: Semele's death and the birth of Dionysus, Ino and Athamas's madness, and the death of Actaeon.

scenes.title: The oracle and the cow
scenes.summary: After Telephassa dies, Cadmus consults Delphi and is told to follow a cow. It leads him through Phocis and Boeotia until it lies down where Thebes now stands.
scenes.stakes: Cadmus has lost his mother and his search for Europa has failed; he must find a place to settle.

scenes.title: The dragon and the Sparti
scenes.summary: Cadmus kills the dragon guarding the spring of Ares and sows its teeth on Athena's advice. The armed men who spring up kill each other, leaving five survivors.
scenes.stakes: Cadmus's companions are being killed by the dragon, and he then faces the armed men.

scenes.title: Marriage of Cadmus and Harmonia
scenes.summary: Cadmus serves Ares for a great year to atone, then receives the kingdom and Harmonia. The gods feast at the wedding, and his children are born and married.
scenes.stakes: Cadmus must atone for killing Ares' dragon.

scenes.title: Semele and Dionysus
scenes.summary: Tricked by Hera, Semele asks to see Zeus as he appears to Hera and is killed by his thunderbolt. Zeus rescues Dionysus; Hera maddens Athamas and Ino, who die, and Dionysus is hidden.
scenes.stakes: Semele risks death by her request; the infant Dionysus and his foster family face Hera's wrath.

scenes.title: The death of Actaeon
scenes.summary: Actaeon, a hunter trained by Chiron, is turned into a deer and eaten by his dogs. The dogs' grief is soothed by an image Chiron makes; the text then breaks into fragments naming the dogs.
scenes.stakes: Actaeon is destroyed by his own hounds after angering a god.

notable_quotes.reason: The famous sowing of dragon's teeth producing the Sparti, the Theban warrior-race.
Zeus's thunderous arrival brings Semele's death and Dionysus's strange birth.

analysis.text: The Theban founding story shows a pattern of divine favour mixed with disaster: Cadmus's city and marriage are blessed, yet his family is struck by divine jealousy and anger.
Apollodorus gathers rival versions (Pherecydes, Acusilaus), reflecting a mythographer's effort to compile and compare traditions.

legacy.text: 'Sowing dragon's teeth' became a proverbial phrase for actions that breed future conflict.
Actaeon's transformation was retold by Ovid and became a frequent subject in European painting, notably by Titian.

fun_facts.text: The section ends with garbled fragments, apparently a quoted poem listing Actaeon's hounds, inserted into the text.

language_notes.text: "Hospitably received" means welcomed and entertained as a guest, a duty central to Greek custom.
"Followed it behind" means he trailed after the cow, letting it choose the route.
"Sank down" means the cow lay down exhausted; "where is now" looks forward to the later city of Thebes.
Sparti means "sown men", from the Greek for sowing; Theban noble families claimed descent from them.
Pherecydes was a Greek mythographer whose version of the myth is cited as an alternative to the main account.
"Eternal year" probably means a great year, a long cycle; the text says it equalled eight ordinary years.
His servitude was the great year (eight years) of service to Ares, imposed to atone for killing the dragon sacred to Ares.
The Cadmea was the citadel of Thebes, said to be founded by Cadmus and named after him.
The necklace of Harmonia is a famous cursed heirloom that later brings disaster to those who own it.
"Abortive" here means born prematurely, before full term; the child is Dionysus.
Rearing Dionysus as a girl was meant to disguise him from Hera's jealous search.
Leucothea and Palaemon were sea deities worshipped as helpers of sailors in distress.
The Hyades, "rainy ones," are a star cluster whose rising was associated with rain.
Acusilaus was an early Greek mythographer; the Artemis version is the better-known story of Actaeon's offence.
"Fashioned an image" means Chiron, the wise centaur, made a likeness of Actaeon, which the dogs mistook for him.
The passage is a broken fragment of quoted verse; the bracketed text is damaged, so its sense is incomplete.

context_notes.text: Delphi was Apollo's oracle, the most authoritative in Greece. Its answers often redirected a seeker's goal, as here.
Athena was goddess of wisdom and war, and a common recipient of sacrifice at the founding of a city.
Ares was the god of war. A dragon guarding his spring explains why killing it later requires atonement.
Harmonia's parentage links Love and War; her marriage to Cadmus was the model of a grand divine wedding.
Zeus appearing to Hera in his full divine form as a storm god makes his lightning lethal to a mortal.
Chiron was the wise centaur who trained heroes such as Achilles and Jason; Cithaeron is the mountain near Thebes.

literary_notes.text: The god answers a different question than the one asked: Cadmus seeks his sister, but is given a new destiny as a city founder.
Warriors born from the earth destroying one another suggests the violence at the root of Thebes' founding.
The narrator offers a rival version, a mythographer's habit that shows the story existed in variants.
Semele's request, prompted by Hera, seems harmless to her but the reader sees it will destroy her.
The hunted deer and boiling cauldron make Hera's induced madness vivid and horrifying.
The dogs' howling search and the comforting image evoke sympathy for the grieving animals.
